Futurists who agree with Lindsey on "generation" hold that it is the generation that sees the signs begin. Those who disagree with him prefer "race" or "kind of people." Both reject the first-century reading.
Does the English word "generation" mean "race," as the Scofield note claimed?
Only as a rare, late-listed sense. Common English use means people living at the same time, as in "generation gap."

The Scofield note claimed that genea, "as does the English word," means primarily race, family or stock. Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary defines generation first as a single step in natural descent, and then as the people living at the same period. It lists "race" only far down the list. The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary also lists "race" last. Everyday speech confirms this. A "generation gap" is a gap between people raised in different times, not between races. On this reading, both the English and the Greek point the same way. The natural sense of "this generation" is the people of that time, and Jesus' prophecy has already become history.
Webster (1828) quotes Luke 9:41, "O faithless and perverse generation," as an example of people living at the same time.
"The World War II generation" means people of a certain era, not a race.

Defenders of the Scofield note say dictionary order does not limit meaning in a theological text. They argue that the phrase "this generation" in the Gospels often carries a moral sense of a kind of people.
If Adam Clarke translated genea as "race," why did he still apply Matthew 24 to AD 70?
Clarke offered no evidence for "race," yet he still held that everything Jesus foretold about the temple and city came true in AD 70.

Adam Clarke, the Methodist commentator, first published his Matthew commentary in 1810. He suggested genea could mean "race" but gave no cross-references for it. Yet he called Matthew 24 a prediction of the utter ruin of the city and temple and the end of the Jewish political state. He said everything Jesus foretold had been fulfilled exactly. On this reading, Clarke's case shows two things. First, the "race" rendering was not created to protect a future fulfillment; even an AD 70 reader used it. Second, modern writers who use "race" to push the chapter into the future cannot claim Clarke's support for their timing. Clarke saw Matthew 24 as strong evidence for the truth of Christianity.
Clarke said the prophecy's fulfillment was among the strongest proofs of the truth of Christianity.
Thomas Newton's Dissertations on the Prophecies (1754) also applied Matthew 24 to AD 70.
Futurists note that Clarke, like many Protestant commentators of his time, did not share modern dispensational assumptions. They grant his AD 70 reading but disagree with it on other grounds.
Was everything in Luke 21:10-24 actually fulfilled by the end of AD 70?
On this reading, yes. The temple was destroyed, the city lay in ruins, many thousands died, and many were taken captive.

Luke records Jesus foretelling wars, earthquakes, famines, persecution of the disciples, armies around Jerusalem, the fall of the city by the sword, captivity among the nations, and Jerusalem trampled by Gentiles (Luke 21:10-24). The South African scholar Norval Geldenhuys noted that by the end of AD 70, about forty years later, these things had happened. Josephus records the siege, the famine, the burning of the temple and the many prisoners sold or sent away (Jewish War 6.9.2-3). On this reading, this is exactly what "before this generation passes away" requires. The historical record matches the prophecy point by point.

Josephus records that 97,000 were taken captive and gives the number of the dead as 1,100,000, many of them pilgrims trapped by the siege (Jewish War 6.9.3). Modern historians think these figures are likely exaggerated, but the loss was immense.
Acts records famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28) and persecution of apostles (Acts 12:1-3), all before AD 70.
Most interpreters agree Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70. Futurists add that "the times of the Gentiles" (Luke 21:24) leaves room for a later section about the end, beginning at verse 25.
Could "this generation" mean a future generation, the one that will see the signs?
This reading says no. Jesus said "this" generation, not "that" one, and spoke to people he told to watch and flee.

One futurist answer is that "this generation" means the generation alive when the signs appear, whenever that is. On this reading, the wording does not allow it. "This" points to something near the speaker. If Jesus meant a far generation, he could have said "that generation," as he said "that day" in verse 36. Every other time Jesus says "this generation" in the Gospels, he means the people around him. And the instructions, to flee Judea and pray the flight is not in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:16-20), fit first-century Judea. Several interpretive models have been offered to avoid the plain meaning, but this reading holds that none fits the grammar as well.
Matthew 24:36 uses "that day" for something future to the speaker, showing Jesus could mark distance when he wished.
Matthew 16:28 makes a similar time promise: "some standing here will not taste death."

Futurists such as John Walvoord and Darrell Bock argued that "this generation" can mean the generation that sees "these things" begin, since the signs themselves define the generation. Bock notes the phrase can point to a kind of people as well as to a time.
What did the disciples ask in Matthew 24:3, and how did they link Jesus' coming with "the end of the age"?
They asked when the temple would fall and what would signal his coming and the end of the age. They saw these as one connected event.

Jesus had just said the house would be left desolate and that all these things would come on this generation (Matthew 23:36-38). He then said not one stone of the temple would be left on another (Matthew 24:2). The disciples asked: when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age? (Matthew 24:3). On the fulfilled reading, they joined the temple's fall, Jesus' coming and the end of the age as one complex event. Jesus did not correct them. The "coming" here is his coming in judgment on Jerusalem. James could therefore tell first-century readers that the Lord's coming was at hand (James 5:8).
Mark 13:4 records the question as "when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be fulfilled?"
Luke 21:7 records it simply about the temple: "when will these things be?"

Many scholars say the disciples mistakenly merged the temple's fall with the end of the world, and Jesus' answer separates the two. Futurists hold that the "coming" in verse 3 is the visible Second Coming.
Does "the end of the age" mean the end of the world?
On this reading, no. The word is aion (age), not kosmos (world). It means the end of the old covenant era, which closed in AD 70.

The disciples asked about the end of the aion, the age. They did not ask about the end of the kosmos, the physical world. The King James Version's "end of the world" has misled many readers. R. T. France explains it as the end of the Jewish age, the move from a national to an international people of God. Milton Terry called it the close of the pre-Messianic age, the crisis that came when the temple fell. On this reading, the only nearby event that fits "end of the age" is the destruction of Jerusalem. Its fall ended the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices, and opened the new covenant age in full.
Matthew 28:20: "I am with you always, to the end of the age," uses the same phrase.
Hebrews 9:26: Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin, meaning in the first century.

Futurists and many traditional readers note that Matthew 13:39-40 links the end of the age with the final harvest and judgment, and Matthew 28:20 promises Christ's presence until history's close. So they take the "end of the age" as the end of the present era at Christ's return.
Did New Testament writers say the end of the ages had already come upon them?
Yes. Paul, Hebrews and Peter all speak of the "last times" or "end of the ages" as their own time.

Paul wrote that the Old Testament examples were written for "us, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ appeared once "at the end of the ages" to put away sin (Hebrews 9:26). Peter says Christ was revealed "in these last times" for your sake (1 Peter 1:20). He also wrote that the end of all things was at hand (1 Peter 4:7). John said it was "the last hour" (1 John 2:18). On the fulfilled reading, these writers lived in the closing period of the old covenant age, roughly AD 30 to 70. Their "last days" were the last days of that age, not the last days of the planet.
Hebrews 1:1-2: God has spoken "in these last days" by his Son.
Acts 2:16-17: Peter says Joel's "last days" prophecy is happening at Pentecost.
Most evangelical scholars agree the "last days" began at Christ's first coming, but say they stretch from then until his return. On this view the whole church age is the last days.
What is "the age to come" in Jesus' teaching?
On this reading, it is the Messiah's age, the new covenant era that followed the old order. It is not only life after the final judgment.

Jesus said blasphemy against the Spirit would not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). Jewish teachers spoke of "this age" and "the age to come," the age the Messiah would bring. The commentator Charles H. H. Wright explained that the Synagogue called the Messiah's period "the world to come." On this reading, "this age" was the age of the law, and "the age to come" is the Christian era the prophets foresaw. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day (John 8:56). Hebrews says its readers had tasted the powers of the age to come (Hebrews 6:5). The old covenant, with animal sacrifice and earthly priests, passed away when the Lamb of God took away sin.
Hebrews 6:5: believers have "tasted... the powers of the age to come."
Ephesians 1:21 speaks of Christ's rule "not only in this age but also in the one to come."

Most interpreters hold that "the age to come" is the eternal state after the return of Christ, partly tasted now through the Spirit. They see an "already and not yet" pattern, with the age to come begun but not completed.
Does Jesus change the subject at Matthew 24:35-36 from AD 70 to his final coming?
Many preterists say yes. This reading says no: verse 35 confirms the preceding prophecy, and verse 36 still speaks of the coming judgment on Jerusalem.

Respected writers such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, and earlier Charles Spurgeon, held that verse 36 begins a new subject: the final coming. This reading respects them but differs. Verse 35, heaven and earth will pass away but my words will not, affirms the certainty of what Jesus just said. Verse 36, no one knows that day and hour, follows straight on. The central topic of the discourse is the desolation of Israel's house (Matthew 23:38). Nothing in the text announces a new topic or a gap of thousands of years. On this reading, "that day" is the day of the judgment Jesus had just described, which would fall within the generation, though its exact day was unknown.
Henry Alford took verse 35 as a solemn confirmation of what came before.
Luke 21:33-36 has the same saying about heaven and earth, followed by a warning to watch so as to escape "these things."

Partial preterists such as Kik and Gentry see a clear transition at verse 36, from near signs to a far, signless coming. Futurists also see a shift, or none at all because they place the entire chapter in the future.
What did Jesus mean by "heaven and earth will pass away" in Matthew 24:35?
On this reading, it means the passing of the old covenant world, the temple-centred order of Israel, which ended in AD 70.

On the covenantal reading, "heaven and earth" in prophecy often stands for a whole ordered world of worship and rule. The temple was built as a small picture of the cosmos. When God judged his people in the Old Testament, an old order fell and a new one rose: new rulers, a new sanctuary. In the same way, the new covenant brought a new priesthood, new sacrifice, new tabernacle (John 1:14) and new temple (John 2:19; Ephesians 2:21). In effect, a new heaven and earth. The falling stars and darkened sun of verse 29 say the same thing in picture form. So verse 35 means that the old world would pass away, but Jesus' words would stand.
Isaiah 51:15-16: God planted the heavens and laid the earth's foundations when he said to Zion, "You are my people."
Jeremiah 4:23-28 describes the land of Judah's ruin as earth "without form and void" and dark heavens.

Most interpreters take Matthew 24:35 as a contrast: the physical universe will one day pass away, but Jesus' words are more lasting still. They link it with 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 21:1 as a future renewal of creation.
How do falling stars and a darkened sun relate to heaven and earth passing away?
They are the same idea in picture form. In prophecy, falling stars mean rulers and powers falling under God's judgment.

Matthew 24:29 says the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall and the powers of heaven will be shaken. On this reading, this is a vivid way of saying "heaven and earth will pass away." In other texts, falling stars stand for fallen powers. Isaiah calls the king of Babylon a fallen day star (Isaiah 14:12). Daniel sees a horn cast down some of the host and stars (Daniel 8:10). Revelation pictures stars falling to the earth (Revelation 6:13; 12:4). Such pictures signal judgment in history. The passing of heaven and earth, then, was the end of the old order led by those who "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8).
Isaiah 13:10 uses darkened sun, moon and stars for the fall of Babylon in 539 BC.
Ezekiel 32:7-8 uses the same images for the judgment of Pharaoh and Egypt.

Futurists accept that Old Testament sun-moon-star language is often figurative, but expect real cosmic disturbances at Christ's return, citing Luke 21:25-26 and Revelation 6:12-14. Some hold both: a symbolic fulfillment in AD 70 and a literal one at the end.
Did respected earlier scholars read "heaven and earth passing away" as the end of the Jewish order?
Yes. John Owen, John Lightfoot and John Brown all read some heaven-and-earth texts as the end of the Mosaic order in AD 70.

The Puritan John Owen (1616-1683) taught that the heaven and earth of 2 Peter 3:5-7 referred not to the final judgment but to the ruin of the Jewish church and state. John Lightfoot (1602-1675), a Hebrew scholar, applied the passing of heaven and earth to the destruction of Jerusalem, as if the whole frame of the world were dissolved. The Scottish expositor John Brown (1784-1858), commenting on Matthew 5:18, said those who know Old Testament language know that the ending of the Mosaic economy is often described as the removal of the old heavens and earth. On this reading, this is not a modern invention. It has a long line of careful Protestant scholars behind it.
Owen preached on 2 Peter 3 in a sermon later printed in his Works, volume 9.
Lightfoot drew on Jewish writings to show how "heaven and earth" language was used for Israel's order.

Many Reformed scholars, including most of Owen's and Lightfoot's contemporaries, applied these texts to the end of history. Others accept the covenantal sense for some passages (like Matthew 24:29) but not for 2 Peter 3 or Revelation 21.
Does the contrast between "this generation" (verse 34) and "that day" (verse 36) show two different events?
This reading says no. "This" fits something present and "that" fits something future to the speaker, whether it is forty years away or far longer.

Kenneth Gentry argued that "this generation" points to what is near and "that day" to what is far. If Jesus meant the same time, he would have said "this day." On this reading, the argument does not hold. "This generation" was the present generation Jesus addressed, so "this" was the right word. The day of judgment was still future to his hearers, so "that" was the right word. The Bauer-Arndt-Gingrich lexicon notes that houtos (this) refers to what is relatively near, and ekeinos (that) to what is relatively farther. A day forty years away is "that day." John Gill read "that day and hour" as the day of vengeance on Jerusalem.
Luke 17:31 speaks of "that day" for the day of the Son of Man, inside the same AD 70-type warnings about fleeing from housetops.
Matthew 7:22: "many will say to me in that day," for a future day.
Gentry and other partial preterists hold the contrast is deliberate and marks a shift to the final coming. Many futurists see the shift too, or read both phrases as future.
If Jesus put the event within his generation, how could he say no one knows "that day and hour"?
Knowing the generation is not knowing the day. Jesus gave a time limit but not the exact date.

Jesus said the events would come before his generation passed, yet the exact day and hour was known only to the Father (Matthew 24:36). These do not conflict. A person can know a harvest will come this year without knowing the date. On this reading, the disciples knew the window but not the day. That is why Jesus told them to pray the flight would not be in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:20). Adam Clarke noted that hora can mean "season," and that the disciples did not know the season either. John Lightfoot said it was a wonder anyone applied these words to the last judgment, since the whole discourse concerns Jerusalem.
A pregnant woman knows her child will come within a few weeks, but not the hour (compare 1 Thessalonians 5:3).
The Roman siege began near Passover AD 70, and the temple burned in late summer. Believers who had fled earlier were spared (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).

Partial preterists and futurists answer that "that day and hour" refers to the final coming, for which no time limit is given. They see verse 36 as a deliberate contrast with the dated events of verse 34.
Why are there fewer signs after Matthew 24:35, if the subject has not changed?
The signs had already been given. After verse 35 the focus moves from signs to watchfulness while waiting.

Some argue that the specific signs of verses 4-34 give way to general warnings after verse 35, so a new event must be in view. On this reading, there are two plain reasons for the change. First, all needed signs had been given. The disciples knew what to look for: false messiahs, armies around Jerusalem, the abomination. Second, the teaching shifts from "what will happen" to "how to live meanwhile." Parables about the flood, the thief, the faithful servant, the ten virgins and the talents all call for readiness. Watching and working are the right response to a known but undated judgment. The change of style is a change of application, not a change of event.
Matthew 24:42-44: the thief in the night calls for alertness.
Matthew 25:13: "watch, for you do not know the day or the hour."

Those who see a transition at verse 36 argue the lack of signs is the very point: the final coming will be without warning, while AD 70 had clear warnings. Futurists also note that the call to watch applies to every Christian generation.
Does the shift from plural "days" to singular "day" mark a new event?
This reading says no. The "days" were the tribulation; the "day" was the climax that followed, when the city fell.

Kenneth Gentry argued that the many "days" of the Great Tribulation contrast with the single "day" of the Second Advent, which comes in a moment (1 Corinthians 15:52). On this reading, this misses the order of the chapter. The tribulation days (Matthew 24:15-28) do not include the collapse of verse 29 or the coming of verse 30. Those come "immediately after the tribulation of those days" (Matthew 24:29). So there were days of tribulation, followed by a certain day of climax, known only to the Father. The Son of Man's coming, like his coming to the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:13, happened at a definite point. Tens of thousands saw the city and sanctuary burn.
Luke 17:26-30 uses the same pattern: "the days of Noah" then "the day" Noah entered the ark.
The temple burned on the tenth of Av (around late August) AD 70, a single day after months of siege (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5).

Gentry and others hold the plural-singular contrast supports a transition. Futurists see the "day" as the visible return after a future tribulation of "days," and read the whole sequence of verses 15-31 as still ahead of us.
What was Jesus' point in comparing his coming to "the days of Noah"?
That life would go on as normal until judgment fell suddenly. Eating, drinking and marrying are ordinary life, not special signs of wickedness.

Jesus said that in the days before the flood people were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood swept them away (Matthew 24:37-39). On this reading, the point is ordinary life, not extreme sin. Some writers, such as M. R. DeHaan and Jack Van Impe, have read "marrying" as wife-swapping. But "marrying and giving in marriage" means simply weddings, as in Matthew 22:30. D. A. Carson notes that there is no mention here of that generation's sins. The same people who lived through the "days before" were caught on "the day." Noah was warned about things "not yet seen" (Hebrews 11:7). Judgment came on people who ignored the warning.
Matthew 22:30: in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, the same phrase used plainly.
Genesis 6:5 records the wickedness of Noah's world, but Jesus' point in Matthew 24 is the people's unreadiness.

Some futurists read the days of Noah as a sign that moral corruption will increase before Christ returns, linking Genesis 6:5 and 2 Timothy 3:1-5. Others agree with Carson that the stress is on normal life and surprise.
Do the buying, selling, planting and building in "the days of Lot" describe moral corruption?
No. They describe normal daily work. The point is that people carried on as if no judgment were coming.

Luke adds the days of Lot: people ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and built, but on the day Lot left Sodom fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all (Luke 17:28-29). Darrell Bock suggests these activities hint at corruption, though he admits Luke does not stress it. On this reading, no one doubts that Sodom was wicked (Genesis 18:20). But Jesus lists ordinary business, not sins. His point is that people lived as though the threat of judgment were empty, just as scoffers later asked where the promised coming was (2 Peter 3:3-4). The same was true of those warned that Christ would judge within a generation.
Luke 17:32: "Remember Lot's wife." She looked back and was lost.
Thomas Newton (1754) compared believers rescued from Jerusalem to Lot rescued from Sodom.

Many commentators agree the stress is on normal life and unpreparedness. Some futurists still see a hint of growing worldliness and indifference before the end, and link it with Paul's warning about lovers of pleasure in 2 Timothy 3:1-5.
Are those "taken" in Matthew 24:39-41 raptured, or taken in judgment?
On this reading, taken in judgment. In Noah's day the flood took the wicked away; Noah's family remained.

The flood came and "took them all away" (Matthew 24:39). Luke says it "destroyed them all" (Luke 17:27, 29). Those taken were the ungodly; Noah and his family remained to carry on God's work. Then Jesus says two will be in the field, one taken and one left (Matthew 24:40-41). In Luke, the disciples ask "Where, Lord?" and Jesus answers that where the body is, the vultures will gather (Luke 17:37). The taken ones end up as corpses. Even dispensationalist John Walvoord agreed that the one taken here is taken in judgment, as in Noah's day. On this reading, the nearest such judgment was AD 70, when Roman armies killed or carried off many people.
Luke 17:37: "Where the body is, there the vultures (or eagles) will gather."
John Gill applied the "taken" to those seized by the Roman army.

Many pretribulationists read "taken" as the rapture, noting that the verb in Matthew 24:40 (paralambano) is used in John 14:3 for Jesus taking believers to himself. Walvoord and others, however, read it as judgment.
Why does Luke 17 put the same sayings in a different order from Matthew 24?
Luke arranges five Olivet sayings in a different sequence. On this reading, it shows they describe one judgment, not a strict two-event timetable.

Luke 17:22-37 contains five sayings found in Matthew 24: the lightning, the days of Noah, the housetop, the one taken and one left, and the vultures. If Matthew's order is 1-2-3-4-5, Luke's is roughly 2-4-1-5-3. Luke puts the Noah analogy before the housetop warning and the lightning. Ray Summers called it a most difficult passage and urged caution. On this reading, if Matthew 24 split cleanly into an AD 70 half and a far-future half, Luke's mixing of the halves would be very strange. It is easier to see all the sayings as describing the same coming in judgment. This is not proof, but it adds weight.
Luke 17:31 (housetop, do not go down) appears in Matthew 24:17, before the "transition" verse.
Luke 17:26-27 (Noah) appears in Matthew 24:37-39, after it.
Others answer that Jesus taught similar things on different occasions, so Luke 17 may record a separate talk. Many scholars see Luke 17 as about the final coming and Luke 21 as about AD 70.
Do "after a long time" (Matthew 25:19) and the bridegroom's delay (Matthew 25:5) mean a delay of thousands of years?
This reading says no. In each parable the master returns to the same servants he left. A "long time" fits within a lifetime.

Some argue these parables show the master's absence is long, so they must describe a distant return. On this reading, the parables set their own limits. The evil servant says, "my master is delayed," and the master returns and punishes that same servant (Matthew 24:48-51). In the talents, after a long time the master settles accounts with the same servants who received the money (Matthew 25:19). The bridegroom comes at midnight to the same virgins who grew drowsy that evening (Matthew 25:5-6). Elsewhere in the New Testament "a long time" means years, not centuries: Herod had wanted to see Jesus for a long time (Luke 23:8). The delay must be measured against the hearers' lives.
John 5:6: the man at the pool had been ill "a long time," thirty-eight years.
Acts 14:28: Paul and Barnabas stayed "a long time" in Antioch.

Most interpreters see the delay in these parables as a hint that the Second Coming would not be immediate, and that the church must stay faithful through a long wait. Parables, they say, do not set exact lengths of time.
Who were the scoffers asking "Where is the promise of his coming?" in 2 Peter 3:3-4?
On this reading, people of the first century who mocked the promise as decades passed before AD 70. The judgment silenced them.

Peter warns that scoffers will come, saying: where is the promise of his coming? Everything continues as it was (2 Peter 3:3-4). On this reading, the setting is the first century. Jesus had said some standing with him would not die before seeing his coming (Matthew 16:27-28). Many believed John might live until then (John 21:22-23). The soon return was common teaching (Philippians 4:5; Hebrews 10:25, 37; Revelation 1:1, 3). As the decades passed, some mocked. The scoffers, like the evil servant, said "my master delays." The judgment of AD 70 answered them within the promised generation.
Hebrews 10:37: "in a very little while, the coming one will come and will not delay."
John 21:22-23: a rumour spread that John would not die before Jesus came.

Most interpreters hold that the scoffers mock the promise of Christ's final return, and Peter answers that with the Lord a thousand years is as a day (2 Peter 3:8). So the delay of many centuries is not a broken promise.
Is the "coming of the Son of Man" in Matthew 24:37-39 different from the coming in verses 27 and 30?
This reading says no. Jesus uses identical words and gives no hint that a second, different coming is in view.

Jesus speaks of "the coming of the Son of Man" in verse 27 (like lightning), verse 30 (on the clouds), verse 37 (as in Noah's days) and verse 39. He uses the same phrase each time. He does not say "this coming" and "that coming" as he does with "this generation" and "that day." On this reading, nothing would lead the disciples to think he was suddenly describing a different coming, separated by thousands of years, when he used the same words minutes later. If two events were meant, one would expect a clear marker. The simplest reading is one coming: Christ's judgment on that generation.
Matthew 24:27 and 24:37 both use parousia, "coming."
Matthew 24:3 asked about "your coming" (singular).
Those who see a transition at verse 36 hold that parousia after that point refers to the final return. Futurists see one coming throughout, but in the future, not AD 70.
Does the judgment of the nations in Matthew 25:31-46 refer to AD 70 or to the end of history?
On this reading, it describes Christ's ongoing judging reign over the nations, which began with his enthronement and continues until every enemy is subdued.

Matthew 25:31 closely matches Matthew 16:27: the Son of Man comes in glory with his angels and repays each person. Matthew 16:28 ties that coming to some who would not taste death first. On this reading, the judgment of the nations is not one single day. Milton Terry argued that Matthew 25:31-46 presents an ideal of judgment over time, tied to Christ's everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:14). Christ was exalted to God's right hand and rules until his enemies are made his footstool (Acts 2:33-35; 1 Corinthians 15:25). The day of judgment for any wicked nation comes when its penalty falls. The King keeps judging among the nations until he has put down all rule and authority.
Psalm 96:10-13: "the Lord reigns... he comes to judge the earth."
